output: Chelsea has made a formal offer for FC Tokyo's 22-year-old forward, Yoshinori Muto, with the aim of acquiring him this summer. If the move to Stamford Bridge is completed, Muto will join Chelsea's Dutch partner club, Vitesse Arnhem, on loan next season. A £4 million deal has been mooted, and Muto has not yet decided whether to join the club, though he considers the offer an honor. Muto is a Japan international with 11 caps and 1 goal, and he recently graduated from Keio University with an economics degree.

Sir Bradley Wiggins, a four-time Olympic champion and 2012 Tour de France winner, will attempt to break the cycling hour record on June 7 at London's Olympic Velodrome. He aims to ride the furthest distance in 60 minutes at the Lee Valley VeloPark, hoping to beat the current record of 52.491km set by Australian Rohan Dennis. Tickets for the event will go on sale from April 19, and the attempt will be broadcast live on Sky Sports.

River Plate is keen to sign Manchester United striker Radamel Falcao, with vice president Matias Patanian stating the club "dream of Falcao" and that "the doors are open." Falcao, who spent eight years with River Plate before moving to Porto in 2009, has struggled during a loan spell at Manchester United this term. It is currently uncertain if United will keep him or if he will return to Monaco. Falcao has recently been in good goalscoring form for Colombia, scoring three times in two games.

The glowing blue letters that lit up Yankee Stadium in the Bronx since 1976 failed to find a buyer at a Sotheby's auction on Wednesday, despite an expected value of $300,000 to $600,000. The only bid, for $260,000, was placed by a Sotheby's employee. The current owner is Yankee Hall of Famer Reggie Jackson, who purchased the 10-feet-tall letters for an undisclosed amount after the stadium's final game in 2008.

Nathan Hughes's three-match ban, initially issued for being "reckless" after his knee collided with George North's head while scoring for Northampton on March 27, has been overturned on appeal. The original disciplinary panel had shown Hughes a red card and issued a ban, despite acknowledging there was no intent. However, the appeal lodged by Wasps was upheld, and the appeal panel concluded that no foul play occurred, as the incident was accidental. Hughes is now free to return to action immediately, though he is not in the squad for Wasps' upcoming trip to London Welsh and is unlikely to play until April 26.

Becky Schoenig of St. Louis, Missouri, had her brand new 2015 Ford Fusion stolen from her driveway on Monday night. On April 1, police found the car after a tip from a man who recognized it, but the vehicle had been modified with red rims, red detailing on the sides, and orange accents on the steering wheel. Instead of being upset, Schoenig thanked the thieves on Facebook for "pimping out" her vehicle. However, the car still needs professional cleaning due to the smell of cigarettes and marijuana. To honor Mick Sexton, who located her car, Schoenig is creating a special smoothie at her restaurant, The Hot Pot.

The parents of the youngest victim of the 2013 Boston Marathon bombings, Bill and Denise Richard, are urging the Justice Department to drop the death penalty for Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, who was convicted on all 30 charges related to the bombings. They argue that pursuing the death penalty would prolong their anguish through years of appeals, and instead support the defendant spending the rest of his life in prison without appeal.

Four-year-old James Hayward had his plastic nerf gun confiscated at East Midlands Airport because it was picked up on the X-ray machines and deemed a security risk. His parents, Phil and Hazel, were traveling to Lanzarote. Security officers frisked James and took the toy, which fires sponge darts, after Phil described the checks as "over-zealous" and "ludicrous." The airport apologized for the inconvenience but stated that their priority is passenger safety and that regulations prohibit items resembling prohibited items. After the holiday, James was bought a replacement toy gun.

Although he recently had a falling out with manager Laurent Blanc after being dropped for a Champions League match, Van der Wiel insists he has no plans to leave and wants to sign a new contract. However, the club remains linked with Dani Alves, and it is uncertain if Van der Wiel will be sold.

Despite past accusations of favouring Louis van Gaal's side, Clattenburg has only sent off two players this Premier League season, both from United (Tyler Blackcett and Luke Shaw). City captain Vincent Kompany is suspended for the match against Wales due to two bookable offences in a Euro 2016 qualifier. An FBI agent's sniper rifle was stolen overnight from his car at the Marriott Springhill Suites hotel parking lot in Salt Lake City, just days before President Obama visited Utah. The rifle, which was secured in a hard case, was reportedly ripped out of the car's window. Police believe the thief broke the rear right passenger-side window, used a rope or cable lock, and used another vehicle's momentum to break the case free. Additionally, the agent's gear bag, backpack, and some clothing and tools were stolen. The rifle has not been recovered, but its serial number has been entered into the National Crime Information Computer.

Everton manager Roberto Martinez defended Ross Barkley taking a penalty against Burnley at Goodison Park, despite Leighton Baines being available. Martinez stated that Barkley was within his rights to request penalty duties, noting that he is happy to have multiple players capable of taking penalties. These satellites would orbit the Earth and use mirrors to harvest sunlight. While initial trials in Scotland were successful, Quarterman plans to move trials to Portugal, though he acknowledges the potential for misuse. Separately, researchers in Tokyo proposed a laser system for the ISS to shoot down space debris up to 62 miles away by pushing it into Earth's atmosphere, but this laser would not be powerful enough to be a weapon.

Shelly Sterling accused Stiviano of targeting wealthy older men and claimed Sterling used their money to purchase luxury items for Stiviano, including a Ferrari, two Bentleys, a Range Rover, and a $1.8 million duplex. Stiviano countered that the gifts were not wrong and that she did not take advantage of Sterling. Shelly Sterling's lawyer stated the court decision is a victory for the Sterling family in recovering the money and sets a precedent for injured spouses to recover damages from gift recipients. He founded the Academy of Ancient Music (AAM) in 1973, directing it for about 30 years, and the AAM produced over 200 CDs, including the first complete cycle of Mozart symphonies on period instruments. His career included positions as an artistic director for the King's Lynn Festival and Boston's Handel and Haydn Society, as well as being a tutor at Harvard and a professor at the University of Cambridge and Cornell University. The New York Times described this policy as "brutal" and "inhumane," noting it contradicts Australia's tradition of welcoming refugees. Washington blamed Russia and the Syrian government for intensifying attacks against civilians in Aleppo, Syria's largest city, which has seen heavy aerial bombardment since the ceasefire ended two weeks ago. The US warned it would halt talks unless Moscow stopped bombing Aleppo, leading Russia to regret the US move and accuse it of shifting blame for the truce's collapse. Fleet Street, once the center of the nation's biggest newspapers and a pinnacle of a journalist's career, is seeing the end of its era. The first British daily newspaper, the Daily Courant, was published there in 1702. At its height, nearly every national paper had offices within a half-mile radius.

Reporters Gavin Sherriff and Darryl Smith, who worked for the Dundee-based Sunday Post, were among the last to work there before the London office closed. Sherriff, who worked there for 32 years, recalled the atmosphere of typewriters and lorries, contrasting it with the current sandwich bars. Smith, who worked there for 25 years, noted the street's history, including its connection to Sweeney Todd's barber shop.

Robin Esser, an ex-Sunday Express editor, stated that at its height, 85% of the public's information came through newspapers because television and social media were in their early stages.

The decline of Fleet Street began when media tycoon Rupert Murdoch moved his papers to Wapping in 1986, leading to a dispute. By 1988, most national newspapers had moved away, adopting computerised printing technology. The buildings have since been repurposed, with some now housing supermarkets or restaurants.

Sylvia Blackburn, a 72-year-old lollipop lady, suffered serious head injuries last December outside Bedford Road Lower School, Kempston, when Brian Wright, 55, struck her. Mrs. Blackburn was on duty escorting a woman and her daughter across the road when Wright's VW Golf failed to stop for a red light. Wright claims he was blinded by the setting sun, which was 10 minutes from setting, and denies causing serious injury by dangerous driving. He has expressed remorse for the incident. Older People's Commissioner for Wales, Sarah Rochira, is conducting a review into the quality of life and care of older people in residential care in Wales. She is calling on pensioners, their families, and friends to share their experiences, which will inform recommendations for care providers and public bodies. The review assesses factors like physical and psychological health, social relationships, and the care home environment, and will also involve speaking with care providers, social care staff, and public bodies. Mario Kreft of Care Forum Wales supported the review's aims but expressed disappointment that no provider expert was included on the main advisory panel.

Matching Models, an international temp agency, faced criticism for its advertisements, which included one for a personal assistant requiring a "classic look, brown long hair with b-c cup," and another for a "sexy female driver." The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) called the assistant ad "appalling, unlawful and demeaning to women," and the Fawcett Society noted it was "straight out of the 1970s."

The agency's founder, Nathalie Jansen, defended the ads by stating that "looks are important" to her clients. Employment lawyer James Lynas described the ads as "clearly unlawful," noting that phrases like "beautiful and attractive" could be discriminatory against older women, and that the EHRC has powers to intervene.

The agency's website stated that it is "almost politically incorrect to request someone to work for you that is both attractive as well as professionally equipped." However, the EHRC suggested the agency should act like a 21st-century business and stop the sexism. Under the 2010 Equality Act, it is illegal to imply discrimination based on various factors, and specifying clothing sizes must be essential to the work. Jansen explained the specific cup size requirement was for a client's designed outfit.

A team, including Dr Neil Loader and Emeritus Prof Alayne Street-Perrott, discovered over 450 large geometrical "geoglyphs" in Acre state, western Brazilian Amazon. Furthermore, the research indicates that the Amazonian forests were not pristine ecosystems but were transformed by humans over 6,000 years through the concentration of economically valuable trees, suggesting a form of "prehistoric supermarket" or "agroforestry."

Horwell suggested the Russian state was likely the sponsor of the plot, noting that the evidence points to Russian state involvement in the murder. The suspects left a "trail of polonium" and had no credible answer to the scientific evidence against them. Attempts to extradite the two men have failed, and they remain in Russia.

Militants, claiming to be from the Islamic State (IS), attacked a hospital in Kabul by detonating explosives at the gate and then opening fire on staff and patients. Commandos killed all four attackers after several hours of fighting, and the defense ministry reported that more than 50 people were wounded. This attack marks a shift in IS's approach in Afghanistan, as it was the first time they engaged directly with security forces in the capital, using a method more associated with the Taliban. IS has previously targeted civilian gatherings and the Supreme Court, while the Taliban has denied involvement.

The English rider crashed at this year's TT, and the Fireblade bike has experienced mechanical issues. Although Martin initially told MCN he was quitting road racing, he later clarified on Facebook that he is not giving up on racing but has no plans to race on Hondas this year. He did not race at the North West 200 because his teammate John McGuinness crashed in practice, and he will not compete in the Ulster Grand Prix. Martin stated that the TT was a disaster and that after testing at Cadwell, he informed the team the bike would not be competitive at the Ulster Grand Prix, leading to his withdrawal from the event. He now wishes to race classics and oddball events.

England won the series with a day to spare at Old Trafford, leveling the series after making 589-8 and 173-1 declared. Joe Root was named man of the match for his performance, scoring 254 in the first innings and an unbeaten 71 in the second, while also taking four catches and a wicket. Captain Alastair Cook scored 105 and 76 not out. Pakistan struggled, batting for only 63 overs in the first innings and 70 in the second on a pitch that offered little assistance. Pakistan's captain, Misbah-ul-Haq, expressed disappointment, noting that shot selection cost them. Pakistan will play a two-day tour game against Worcestershire before the third Test at Edgbaston on August 3rd.

President Ivanov cancelled an investigation into abuse of power claims revealed by covert recordings, stating he wanted to "put an end to the agony" before the June elections. This move was condemned by the opposition and EU officials, who noted it was not in line with the rule of law and risked Macedonia's EU membership ambitions. The crisis began in 2015 after recordings surfaced, allegedly showing ministers plotting vote-rigging and covering up a murder. Opposition leader Zoran Zaev has since released recordings accusing the government of wiretapping 20,000 people and revealing high-level corruption, while the government denies these accusations and accuses Zaev of trying to destabilize the nation.

The former Reds captain, Steven Gerrard, is returning to his former club as a youth coach in February, marking his first job since retiring as a player. Klopp described the appointment as "wonderful news" and noted that Gerrard wants to be a manager in the future, stating he is ready to take steps to learn the job. Gerrard, who retired after a 19-year career, made his Liverpool debut in 1998 and left for LA Galaxy in 2015. He is currently working towards his UEFA A coaching licence, which is necessary to manage in the Premier League.

Adrian Gill, a journalist and writer, died this morning after being diagnosed with "the full English" of cancers. He joined the Sunday Times in 1993 and was described by colleagues as a "giant among journalists," the "heart and soul" of the paper, and a brilliant, fearless writer. Gill, who overcame dyslexia, began his career in the 1980s with art reviews before writing for Tatler and the Sunday Times. His career was marked by popular writing that often caused controversy, including comments about the Welsh, the Isle of Man, and Clare Balding. He was married twice; his first marriage was to Cressida Connolly in 1983, and his second was to Amber Rudd in 1991. His illness led to his engagement to Nicola Formby, with whom he had two children.

Amarmandakh Sukhbaatar, the lead singer of Khar Sarnai, was allegedly attacked in Ulan Bator while performing. Russian news reports stated he was hit over the head with a bottle and repeatedly kicked in the face, resulting in him spending about 10 days in a coma. The rapper wore a red deel embroidered with a swastika, a symbol he emphasized is a traditional Mongolian symbol predating Hitler, though it is also used by some far-right groups. The Russian embassy is investigating the assault but claims local press reports are "distorted." The suspect is identified as a Russian diplomatic officer, who was not detained because his injuries were not considered serious.

Craig Hughes, 33, of Flint, was arrested by North Wales Police in August after chatting online with the Hope Line Crisis Centre in Tennessee. He admitted to two charges at Mold Crown Court for planning a murder bid involving the ambush of police after reporting a non-existent crime. Hughes stated he intended to shoot officers on the Dee Estuary after they arrived at the scene. The threats were made while he was drunk, and Judge Niclas Parry remanded him in custody pending sentence, noting his previous firearm conviction.

Three Victorian hotels—Bay View Court, The Cottonwood, and the Ocean View—will be demolished at East Cliff in Bournemouth to make way for a six-storey, four-star hotel and two assisted-living apartment blocks. English Heritage strongly objected to the development's scale in the designated conservation area, but councillors voted seven to three in favor, citing the need to improve tourism and living conditions for older people. The project, proposed by The East Cliff Project LLP, will also include a 90-room hotel and a nine-storey and seven-storey building with 122 assisted-living apartments.

Italian consumer organisations have filed a formal complaint with the European Commission, accusing McDonald's of forcing franchisees to pay excessive rents and high fees. The complaint, supported by the SEIU and European unions, claims that franchisees are prevented from switching to competitors due to long-term contracts and that they lease premises from McDonald's at above market rates, which allegedly leads to poorer consumer choice and higher prices. McDonald's defends its practices, stating it shares risks and rewards with its licensees, an approach it claims has been successful. The European Commission has stated it will study the submission and may launch an investigation if the allegations are founded.

The House of Lords European Union Committee report examines the risks and opportunities for the UK fishing industry following Brexit. While the industry hopes Brexit will allow it to regain control of UK waters and become a leading fish-exporting nation, the report warns that the industry risks being marginalized in negotiations. Key challenges include the fact that most commercial fish stocks are in shared waters with EU states, and that continued market access is needed for a successful industry. Potential trade-offs may involve EU member states demanding more access to UK waters in exchange for continued zero-tariff access to the European market. The report also suggests retaining elements of the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP) and basing catches on scientific advice, while noting the potential for four different fisheries management regimes post-Brexit. Despite these concerns, some industry representatives remain optimistic, viewing Brexit as an opportunity for fairer shares and better management of the 200-mile exclusive economic zone.

In 2011, the poverty rate was 15%, affecting 46.2 million Americans, which was flat after three years of increases. Real median household income decreased by 1.5%, and the average poverty threshold for a family of four was $23,021 (£14,300). Income inequality rose by 1.6% in 2011, marking the first annual increase since 1993. Additionally, the percentage of Americans without health insurance fell to 15.7% from 16.3%, following a record high poverty rate of 15.1% in 2010.

The 25-year-old cricketer, Buttler, moved to the Red Rose from Somerset in 2013 and is contracted until 2019. He is a short-format specialist who has scored England's three fastest ODI centuries, including a 46-ball ton against Pakistan last year. Cricket director and head coach Ashley Giles praised Buttler's talent, noting his contribution to winning last year's T20 Blast final and his positive influence on the squad. Buttler, who plays for Mumbai Indians in the Indian Premier League, will return to Lancashire for a T20 Blast home game against Durham.

Deputy Foreign Minister Faisal al-Mekdad stated that Syria is doing its best to comply with the timetable to destroy its chemical weapons, despite missing Wednesday's deadline to hand over its entire stockpile. He attributed the delay to two shipments of weapons being attacked on their way from Damascus to Latakia, with the second shipment intercepted by terrorist groups.

Regarding the conflict, Mr. Mekdad described US Secretary of State John Kerry's condemnation of the use of barrel bombs in Aleppo as "absolutely unacceptable," while the Syrian government denied reports of rebels seizing most of Aleppo's central prison. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights and the Aleppo Media Centre reported that fighting continues and that rebels control the prison, which holds at least 3,000 detainees.

The chemical weapons destruction process, overseen by the OPCW, has been slowed by security concerns. Syria has about 1,300 tonnes of declared chemical weapons, and the US reported that only about 4% of the stockpile had left the country. Russia has urged Damascus to complete the transfer of chemical weapons to the coast by March 1st, with a final destruction deadline set for the end of June.

Mukherjee's *The Lives Of Others*, set in 1960s Calcutta, is the favourite to win the Booker Prize, which is now open to all English-language authors regardless of nationality. The winner will be announced at London's Guildhall on Tuesday night. The shortlist includes Howard Jacobson, Ali Smith, Joshua Ferris, Karen Joy Fowler, and Richard Flanagan. Jacobson is nominated for his futuristic love story *J*, while Smith's *How To Be Both* tells two interlinking stories. Ferris's *To Rise Again at a Decent Hour* examines atheism through a New York dentist's perspective, and Fowler's *We Are All Completely Beside Ourselves* narrates the story of a family with a surprisingly special child. Flanagan's *The Narrow Road to the Deep North* is a love story set during the construction of the Thailand-Burma Death Railway in World War Two. Fowler's book is the best-selling on the list, having sold over 55,000 copies since its March publication.

Lawrence Phillips, a former star player at the University of Nebraska and an NFL player for the St Louis Rams, Miami Dolphins, and San Francisco 49ers, is believed by officials to have killed himself early on Wednesday. Despite his athletic career, Phillips faced significant legal troubles, including convictions for assault related to driving into teenagers and assaulting a former girlfriend. He was serving a sentence of over 30 years when he was accused of killing a former cellmate, and a judge found enough evidence to try him in the death of Damion Soward, 37. His former Nebraska coach, Tom Osborne, noted that while Phillips was intelligent and had good qualities, he struggled with anger issues and "demons in his life."

The passage discusses a shift in Northern Ireland's planning system where, from April 2015, local councils will take over the responsibility for making planning decisions, moving away from the Planning Service under Stormont's environment department.

Michael Corr of PLACE is optimistic, viewing this as an opportunity for councils to develop community plans, though he notes that voters must choose politicians capable of understanding urban regeneration. Conversely, Friends of the Earth express concerns, citing historical discrimination in the 1960s and warning that a lack of transparency could lead to unfair planning permissions for certain communities due to close relationships between developers and political parties. They argue for rigorous enforcement of a code of conduct and increased public knowledge of political donations.

The new legislation in Bolivia, signed by Vice-President Alvaro Garcia Linera, permits 12-year-olds to work with parental authorization and establishes a 30-year jail sentence for child homicide. This law reflects Bolivia's needs as one of South America's poorest countries and aims to help eradicate extreme poverty, as over 500,000 children currently work to supplement family income. While the International Labour Organisation (ILO) states children under 15 should not work, the law allows a minimum working age of 14 for developing countries. Mr. Garcia stated that the law balances reality with international treaties, despite the ILO studying whether it breaches international regulations.

Che Labastide-Wellington, a boy from Harrow, was stabbed to death in an alleyway at about 00:30 GMT after a fight with youths who tried to enter a party in Belvedere Way, Kenton. Police believe he was targeted later, despite being invited to the event. A 21-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of murder, and three minors (aged 15, 16, and 14) have also been arrested in connection with the incident.

Avon and Somerset Police closed the Lower Bristol Road in Bath at Rackfield Place outside the First depot following a crash at 03:00 GMT. The A36 road closure, which lasted until 14:00 GMT, caused delays for commuters and bus services during rush hour. Investigations into the collision are ongoing. First reported that while some services resumed normal schedules, it would take several hours for all services to return to normal, with the hope of having full service running for the evening commute.

Hilary won the Theakstons Old Peculier Crime Novel of the Year Award in Harrogate for her book, *Someone Else's Skin*, which is the first in a series featuring Det Insp Marnie Rome and tackles domestic violence and honour crime. Alison Graham described the book as "emotionally exhausting and powerful," while Ann Cleeves praised it for being "finely written and tightly written" and for its well-plotted subject matter. US author Sara Paretsky received an outstanding contribution honour for her 23-year career writing about the female private investigator VI Warshawski, whom Cleeves called a "real game changer" for changing how readers viewed female writers.

Third-party software was allegedly used to steal intimate photos from iCloud, prompting suggestions that Apple implement a safety measure to prevent this. This measure involves an extra step after entering a username and password on a new device, requiring a four-digit code sent via text or the Find My iPhone app. If the code is not entered, access to iCloud and purchases are blocked, though a 14-character recovery key can be used to regain access if the trusted device is lost or stolen.

Previously, two-step verification did not prevent attackers from downloading complete backups using tools like Elcomsoft's Phone Password Breaker. Apple has since implemented changes that guard against this technique, and the account owner now receives an email notification when a backup starts downloading. However, experts have raised concerns about the recovery key being hard to remember or stolen, and one expert suggested that two-factor authentication should be the default setting for all users. Apple plans to more aggressively encourage users to enable two-factor authentication and use stronger passwords.

Mr. Ashley has been asked to provide evidence regarding the treatment of workers at a Derbyshire company following a BBC investigation into the warehouse's working practices. Hartlepool MP Iain Wright, who chairs the Business, Innovation and Skills (BIS) select committee, has invited Mr. Ashley to a meeting at the company's base in Shirebrook. Mr. Wright's letter states the committee will review low-paid worker treatment and the national minimum wage, and notes that Mr. Ashley has not accepted any alternative dates offered. If Mr. Ashley fails to agree to attend, the committee reserves the right to take further action, including seeking support from the House of Commons for a contempt complaint. Sports Direct has not responded to the BBC, though the company previously pledged to review worker rights under Mr. Ashley's oversight.

The passage describes the introduction of the iPhone, which marked a significant shift from phones used only for calls. The author witnessed the unveiling and later used the device for a news piece, which drew commentary. The smartphone has since become a transformative technology, putting powerful computers into the hands of over two billion people and disrupting various industries, particularly photography, by changing how people capture and share images on the move. While mobile devices existed before 2007, Steve Jobs's genius was realizing that an attractive user interface was necessary for people to use their phones for more than just talking and texting. The author concludes that the mobile connected era began on a sunny January morning in San Francisco.

The new divorce application form in England and Wales asks for the name of the person a spouse has committed adultery with, though the Ministry of Justice states there is "no obligation" to name them. Family lawyers and experts express concern that including this information increases "conflict and complexity" and that many applicants may feel pressured to fill in the box. If a third party is named, they become part of the court case, which can potentially delay proceedings and increase costs. While adultery was the reason for 12,148 of the over 100,000 divorces granted in 2015, lawyers note that judges view petitioners trying to involve new partners in proceedings negatively.

Ministers are encouraging commercial forestry investment, but there is a conflict between environmental policy and the timber industry. While Britain is a major wood importer and the industry is worth over £450m to the Welsh economy, Confor warns that 16,000 hectares of commercial forest have been lost since 2001 and need replanting. Ministers want more native broadleaf species and better public access, while conservationists argue commercial forests are detrimental to wildlife. The Welsh government aims for a balance between environmental, economic, and social factors through initiatives like the Glastir scheme, though Confor argues the current system is too bureaucratic and the emphasis on environmental aspects is prioritized over commercial forestry.

Wilson rejoined Forest from Celtic for £2.5m in August 2013, but has been without a team since being released in May. The 30-year-old made 51 appearances in his second spell at the City Ground, following four seasons at the club before moving to Celtic. His previous clubs include Preston North End and Notts County.

The British supermarket giant Tesco is disposing of its loss-making US food chain, Fresh & Easy, which has operated 200 stores in California, Nevada, and Arizona since 2007. The deal involves transferring around 4,000 of Fresh & Easy's 5,000 employees to the new business, Yucaipa, a Los Angeles-based private equity company run by Ron Burkle. Tesco will loan Yucaipa approximately £80m, and while the remaining 50 stores are expected to close, Tesco faces a total disposal cost of £150m. Tesco also retains the option to buy a stake if Yucaipa becomes profitable.
The passage mentions that an individual, who initially faced racial abuse, has overcome it and is now aiming for a medal at the 2016 Rio Olympics, after briefly considering representing France.

Widnes led at half-time 14-6, but Castleford responded with tries from Paddy Flynn, Ah Van, Lloyd White (2), and Joe Mellor to make the score 38-12. Despite three tries in four minutes by Larne Patrick, Luke Gale, and Flynn's hat-trick, Widnes held on to secure a victory. The Vikings' win was made difficult by a defensive lapse allowing Patrick a try, and a nervy finish involving Gale and Flynn. This defeat marked Castleford's fourth consecutive home league loss, while Widnes moved to seventh place, with Castleford remaining in sixth.

The House of Lords European Union Committee has released a report examining the risks and opportunities for the UK fishing industry following Brexit. While the industry has campaigned for Brexit to regain control over UK waters, the report warns that the industry risks being marginalized in negotiations. Key issues include the potential for EU member states to demand more access to UK waters in exchange for continued market access to the EU, and the possibility of four different fisheries management regimes emerging in the UK. Despite these concerns, some industry members remain optimistic about the opportunities for fairer shares and sustainable management.

Tests confirmed that all cats near Victor Avenue in Melton Mowbray, Leicestershire, had ingested a toxic substance. Seven-month-old Meereen died on Monday after being found foaming at the mouth and trying to vomit; vets confirmed she had consumed antifreeze. Three other cats have died in the last seven days, and another died two weeks ago. An RSPCA spokesman stated it is unclear if the poisonings were accidental or deliberate, and an inspector is appealing for the safe storage of pesticides and chemicals, particularly antifreeze used in cars.

Mike Nesbitt, at the end of his party's manifesto launch, stated that "Domination doesn't work, partnership does." While Ulster Unionists want the election to be a referendum on the Renewable Heat Incentive debacle, the focus has shifted to Nesbitt's comments. When asked about Danny Kennedy distancing himself from his remarks, Nesbitt said it was "quite reaffirming to know Danny was listening." Nesbitt denied any regrets or mistakes regarding his statements, asserting he would not withdraw a word and was focused on post-election outcomes. He stated he would rather go into Stormont with the SDLP than Sinn Féin. His manifesto, titled 'Real Partnership', includes calls to tackle waiting lists, increase PSNI numbers to 7,500, prioritize the York Street interchange, support the LGBT community, and guarantee no group is worse off due to Brexit. Furthermore, under 'Cleaning Up Stormont', the party calls for action against "incompetence, arrogance, cronyism and the strong whiff of corruption."

The passage describes two individuals: a 30-year-old former Manchester City player who earned 61 caps for England after debuting in 2009, participated in two World Cups and two European Championships (playing only three minutes at Euro 2016), and a person named Milner, who holds the record for the most capped England Under-21 player with 46 caps since 2004, and scored his only international goal in a 5-0 victory over Moldova at the 2014 Fifa World Cup qualifiers. Additionally, Milner expressed well wishes for Sam Allardyce, the players, staff, and supporters.

Christopher Hogwood, a highly influential exponent of the early-music movement and a founder of the Academy of Ancient Music (AAM) in 1973, died at his Cambridge home after a long illness. He worked with leading orchestras globally and directed the AAM across six continents for about 30 years, which produced over 200 CDs, including the first complete cycle of Mozart symphonies on period instruments. His career included positions as a keyboard player and musicologist with the Academy of Saint Martin-in-the-Fields, and he served as the artistic director for the King's Lynn Festival and Boston's Handel and Haydn Society. He was also a tutor at Harvard, an honorary professor at Cambridge, and a professor-at-large at Cornell University.

The All Progressives Congress (APC) won 19 of the 28 governor posts in the recent elections, marking a significant defeat for the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), which also lost the presidential poll for the first time. APC leader Muhammadu Buhari is set to be inaugurated on May 29th. The PDP's decline is evident as it lost in key northern states like Katsina and Kaduna, and lost control of Adamawa, though it retained Rivers State. The APC has made historic gains, relegating the PDP to a regional party, which performed best in the south-east and the Niger Delta. While the APC won most northern states and Lagos, it failed to win in any of Nigeria's five oil-producing states. The elections were generally more peaceful than in previous years, though violence occurred in some areas.

Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe was sentenced to five years in jail in September for allegedly plotting to topple the government in Tehran. Her husband, Richard Ratcliffe, has criticized the UK government for a lack of action and stated that the appeal against the sentence is being held in Tehran in secret. Mrs. Zaghari-Ratcliffe, 38, has been in solitary confinement since her arrest in April, while her two-year-old daughter, Gabriella, remains in Iran under the care of her grandparents. Mr. Ratcliffe believes his wife is being used as a bargaining chip in a diplomatic row between Iran and the UK, and he is trying to obtain a visa to visit them. Amnesty International UK views Mrs. Zaghari-Ratcliffe as a "prisoner of conscience."

Barry Pring, 47, was killed by a speeding car on the hard shoulder of a dual carriageway in Kiev in 2008 while trying to hail a taxi. The coroner, Dr. Elizabeth Earland, recorded a verdict of unlawful killing, stating she was satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that Barry John Pring was unlawfully killed. His wife, Ganna Ziuzina (Anna), who was 19 years younger, tried to claim his assets shortly after his death. His family believes the death was a staged hit and run, and his mother alleged Ms. Ziuzina was involved to inherit his money, noting she was a lap dancer and stripper. The inquest heard Ms. Ziuzina sold his Range Rover and moved funds from his bank account, and computer records showed she was having an affair with a Ukrainian man. Ukrainian police closed the initial inquiry but relaunched it in 2011 as a murder inquiry, which is currently active but not actively pursued.

Chelmsford Prison has reported numerous incidents of packages being thrown over the wall, with one former inmate claiming the jail is notorious for being flooded with mobile phones and synthetic cannabis. A local resident witnessed packages being thrown over the wall four times in two weeks. While the Ministry of Justice stated staff work hard to stop contraband, the Justice Secretary has asked for ways to ensure prisons have the tools to tackle these issues. Although a former inmate claimed drones were used to fly contraband to prison windows, the Ministry of Justice found no evidence of drones at the Chelmsford site. New laws allow people who smuggle packages over prison walls to be jailed for up to two years.

Del Potro secured a 3-6 6-3 7-6 (7-2) 6-3 victory over the Swiss player, Wawrinka, in his first Grand Slam since the Australian Open in 2014 after three wrist operations. The 27-year-old Argentine, who is currently 165th in the rankings, will next play either Lucas Pouille or Donald Young. In the same half of the draw as Andy Murray, Nick Kyrgios defeated Dustin Brown in a rain-affected second-round match. Kyrgios is set to face Feliciano Lopez in the third round, and the winner will play Murray or John Millman in the last 16. Other results included Tomas Berdych beating Benjamin Becker and Jo-Wilfried Tsonga defeating Juan Monaco.

Tunisia faced expulsion from the 2017 Africa Cup of Nations after lodging complaints against the organization, but they avoided disqualification after apologizing to Caf. Morocco was able to enter the 2017 Nations Cup qualifying draw after the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) overturned a ban on its participation. Morocco had been punished in February for refusing to host the 2015 Nations Cup due to Ebola virus fears, leading to Equatorial Guinea stepping in. Cas later reduced a fine imposed on Morocco's FA. The incident involving Tunisia's row with Caf stemmed from a contentious penalty awarded in their quarter-final against Equatorial Guinea in 2015.

Luke Rockhold is set to face Lyoto Machida in a middleweight clash in New Jersey on Saturday. Rockhold is seeking his fourth consecutive victory and a title shot, stating his plan is to "be the bull" and dominate Machida, who he describes as a "matador." Rockhold believes Machida has a small avenue to win on the feet, while he has a big avenue, noting Machida has little chance on the ground. Machida, who is coming off a victory, is confident he can upset Rockhold and earn a title shot, believing his style and technique can stop Rockhold. Both fighters have recently won their respective fights.

Manuel Pellegrini has expressed disappointment in Yaya Toure's performance this season but has vowed to support the midfielder until the end of the season. Manchester City is reportedly open to offers for Toure as they look to overhaul their aging squad. Toure, who has two years left on his contract, has acknowledged his underperformance and dismissed claims that he needs a rest. Additionally, City is interested in signing West Ham left-back Aaron Cresswell in the summer, though Sam Allardyce has warned Cresswell against making a similar move to City.

Domenico Rancadore, a Sicilian mafia fugitive known as the "godfather of Uxbridge," will remain in the UK after his extradition to Italy was dropped. Rancadore, who has lived in Britain for over 20 years, was given a seven-year sentence by an Italian court in 1999 for being a member of the cosa nostra. His case expired last October, and his European arrest warrant is to be withdrawn because Italian law states that a sentence is extinguished once a period of more than double the time of the penalty has passed. His solicitor, Karen Todner, stated that the Italian court of appeal agreed to extinguish the conviction on the basis that the conviction is too old to sustain a prison sentence.

Rory McIlroy aims to win the Masters to complete the career grand slam, becoming one of only six players to win all four major titles. He views winning the Masters as a career-long goal and believes it is "unthinkable" to finish his career without winning a green jacket. McIlroy is hoping to achieve this at Augusta later this month, following his final-round collapse at Augusta National in 2011, which he considers the most important day of his career because of what he learned from it.

In the past 12 months, 272 youngsters in England were hospitalised with foetal alcohol syndrome, according to the official health and social care information centre. Experts warn the actual number affected by maternal drinking could be higher. Research by the World Health Organisation suggests at least one in 100 babies born in the UK could suffer learning, behavioural, and physical problems, such as deformed limbs, due to alcohol exposure, equating to about 7,500 every year. Children born with the syndrome do not get better, and the condition is vastly under-diagnosed. Other associated medical issues include problems with the liver, kidneys, heart, cerebral palsy, sight loss, and epilepsy.

An axe-wielding robber, Shaun Andrew Mckerry, was jailed after his attempt to rob a store in Shildon, County Durham, on March 15 was foiled. Mckerry, a 31-year-old ex-juvenile offender known as "boomerang boy," entered the post office and stores at 8 pm, waving an axe and demanding cash from assistant Andrea Brighty. Store owner Sab Dhillon tackled Mckerry to the floor, and his wife, Sam, hit him twice with a baseball bat to disarm him. Police arrived minutes later to arrest Mckerry, who had previously pleaded guilty to attempted robbery and was jailed for six years. Mckerry, from Coundon, earned his nickname because he always returned home after committing crimes.

Rail firms are facing criticism for planning fare hikes of up to 87 per cent just ten days after the general election, despite pledges from main party leaders to freeze prices. The Prime Minister, David Cameron, has requested that First Great Western (FGW) urgently review plans to almost double some fares on the London to Cotswolds route, which passes through his constituency. For example, an off-peak return from Charlbury to London is set to increase from £33.30 to £62.40 on May 17. Other planned hikes include an off-peak first-class single from Crewe to Northampton rising from £30 to £37, and an anytime return between Stafford and Liverpool with Virgin increasing from £26.50 to £33. Virgin has stated that the majority of its price hikes affected its "trains-only fares," which are at least 20 per cent cheaper than rival tickets.

Terrorists are undergoing training in rural areas of West Wales, specifically in Ceredigion, Powys, and Pembrokeshire, where they are also being radicalized. An officer from the Wales Extremism and Counter Terrorism Unit noted that those involved in these activities participate in seemingly ordinary community activities but have an ulterior motive. Incidents of Islamic extremist activity in Wales date back to 1998, when a group of 10 extremists trained in the Brecon Beacons in Powys.

Adam Gadahn, known as "the American mouthpiece of al qaeda," was a prominent member of the terrorist organization who spoke against his native country. He was killed in a U.S. government counterterrorism operation in January. Gadahn, born in 1978, converted to Islam in 1995 and moved to Pakistan three years later. He rose through the ranks in the tribal areas of Pakistan, becoming al qaeda's chief official English-language propagandist, and appeared in videos threatening attacks on various interests. He was indicted in 2006 for treason and material support to al qaeda.

A beach-side apartment complex in the Hamptons, the Sandpiper complex, was obliterated by flames on Wednesday afternoon. The fire spread through 90 condos, eventually causing the building to collapse. The blaze was intense, melting paint off nearby buildings and producing smoke visible from three miles away. Twelve fire crews were deployed, but they could not get inside the summer homes, and firefighters used cranes to approach the fire. The cause of the blaze is under investigation, with claims that it may have started near a car parked by the complex. The complex is used as a holiday home by residents between May and November.

A major study by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation at the University of Washington found that heavy drinking and binge drinking among Americans have increased, with heavy drinking rising 17.2 percent between 2005 and 2012. This increase is largely attributed to rising rates among women, driven by changing social norms. In 2012, 8 percent of Americans were heavy drinkers and 18 percent were binge drinkers.

Heavy drinking is defined as exceeding one drink per day for women and two drinks per day for men in the past month, while binge drinking is defined as four or more drinks for women and five or more drinks for men on a single occasion in the past month.

Experts suggest several reasons for the increase, including changing social norms making it more acceptable for women to drink like men, the influence of affluent professionals in cities, the real-dollar decrease in the cost of alcohol due to taxes not rising with the consumer price index, increased alcohol advertising, and the weakening of alcohol control policies.

Michelle Filkins, 44, of West Wareham, was arrested on April 17 after being found by owner Mark Conklin in his summer home on Martha's Vineyard. She is charged with breaking and entering, larceny over $250, and malicious destruction of property. Filkins allegedly lived in the home for at least a week and sold items belonging to the owners in a yard sale. Missing items include various furniture, lamps, a painting, and other household goods. She is scheduled to be in court on May 14.

A lost iPhone belonging to Bella Brooke of Melbourne was reunited with its owner after Albury police officers used the unlocked phone to post a series of humorous selfies and messages on her Facebook page to track her down. The phone was handed in to the Albury police station on the NSW-Victoria border on Sunday morning after Bella lost it at a friend's birthday party the previous night. The police used the phone to post updates, including a picture of it in a holding cell, and reassured Bella that it was safe and fully charged. Bella eventually reclaimed her phone, noting that the officers recognized her from her Facebook page.

A Palestinian teenager, Mohammed Abu Khdeir, whose name appeared on an Israeli memorial at Mount Herzl, is being removed from the wall following complaints from his family and the organization Almagor. Abu Khdeir, 16, was beaten and burned alive by three Israelis in July. His father, Hussein Abu Khdeir, objected to his son's name being listed among soldiers of the occupation, and Almagor opposed his inclusion, describing his death as a rogue attack rather than a terror victim. Almagor demanded his name be removed, threatening to have their own family members' names removed if it was not done. Israel radio reported that the national insurance institute of Israel will remove his name after the father's complaints, and the name has already been removed from the organization's website.

A California-based YouTube user named Lionel Hutz filmed his young son chasing his family cat in the garden to use the cat's belly as a pillow for rest. The cat would lick its fur before the boy would lie on top, but after a brief moment, the cat would get up and move to another spot, which the boy would then follow. This sequence repeated a few times before the cat wandered indoors. Later, the duo was seen making up, with the boy gently feeding the cat treats.

A police corruption trial in Philadelphia is ongoing, but witness Robert Kushner has been handed a losing verdict. Kushner, 32, is one of over a dozen former drug dealers testifying against the federal government regarding police wrongdoing. He lost his varsity coaching job at the Jack M. Barrack Hebrew Academy after testifying that undercover officers stole $81,000 in cash and 7 pounds of marijuana from him during a 2007 arrest. Kushner acknowledged being arrested again in 2011 and pleading guilty to driving under the influence in 2008.

Dani Alves is set to leave Barcelona this summer after rejecting the club's final contract offer. The 31-year-old Brazilian right-back, who has won four Spanish titles and two Champions Leagues in seven years, was unable to agree on a new deal. His agent, Dinorah Santana, stated that the client rejected a three-year contract extension that required him to play in 60% of matches for the club, and that negotiations are now over.

Pablo Osvaldo has urged Italian legends Andrea Pirlo and Francesco Totti to join him at Argentinian club Boca Juniors. Osvaldo believes Pirlo and Totti would be a good fit for Boca due to their South American style and abilities, and he feels the fans would love to see them play at La Bombonera.

The University of Michigan is proceeding with a screening of the film "American Sniper" as part of the UMix social events series, despite a petition from over 200 students who objected to the showing. The film features Bradley Cooper as Chris Kyle, a Navy SEAL sniper who was killed in 2013. Some students opposed the screening because they felt the movie's depiction of the Iraq War negatively portrayed the Middle East and its people. Following a backlash against the initial decision to cancel the showing, the university's vice president for student life stated that canceling the screening was a mistake and that the show will continue, emphasizing the university's value of freedom of expression. UMix will also offer a screening of "Paddington" for those who do not wish to see "American Sniper."

Two French tourists allegedly set a quokka alight on Rottnest Island off Perth, Western Australia, on April 3 by igniting an aerosol spray with a lighter. The quokka survived but was singed. The two men, aged 18 and 24, were evicted from the island and charged with animal cruelty, with their court appearance scheduled for April 17.

At age 75, Jack Nicklaus achieved a hole-in-one on the 130-yard fourth during the par-3 contest at Augusta National. He was playing alongside Gary Player and Ben Crenshaw. While this was Nicklaus's first ace at Augusta, it was eclipsed by Camilo Villegas, who also made two hole-in-ones that day, leveling the record from 2002. Nicklaus has won the Masters multiple times, including becoming the youngest person to wear a green jacket in 1963 and collecting his sixth in 1986. He is one of five men to complete the career grand slam.

A species of whale feared extinct, the Omura's whale, was found washed up on a remote beach in West Australia after Tropical Cyclone Olwyn. This is the first sighting of the species in WA and the second in Australia. Initially difficult to identify, the 5.68 m juvenile female was confirmed as an Omura's whale using DNA profiling. The find is significant because little was known about the species, which was only described in scientific journals in 2003 and is typically found in tropical and subtropical waters, such as Indonesian waters, the Philippines, and the Sea of Japan. The whale has a sleek body shape and unique skeletal features, including 53 or 60 vertebrae and four digits on each pectoral fin. The carcass has been buried, and the skeleton will be recovered in a few years for further scientific investigation.

Leonie Granger, a 25-year-old aspiring model from Gillingham, Kent, was jailed for 16 years for manslaughter over the death of professional gambler Mehmet Hassan, 56. Granger used her looks to befriend Hassan, who showered her with gifts and trips. After Hassan took her to his flat, she left the door unlocked, allowing her boyfriend Kyrron Jackson and accomplice Nicholas Chandler to enter. They tied up Hassan, kicked him to death, and ransacked his home for his hidden winnings. Granger was found guilty of manslaughter by a majority, while Jackson and Chandler were found guilty of murder and jailed for life with a minimum term of 36 years. All defendants were also convicted of robbing Hassan and conspiracy to falsely imprison him.

West Ham is in discussions to sign Jamaican starlet Deshane Beckford, a 17-year-old forward from Montego Bay United, after he impressed during a two-week trial with the club. Beckford, who is considered one of the hottest prospects from the Caribbean, also has offers from Belgian clubs. Additionally, West Ham has revealed that season tickets at the Olympic Stadium will cost as little as £289 for the 2016-20 season, aiming for the cheapest pricing strategy in the Barclays Premier League.

An Arsenal fan made his girlfriend, Saskia, take a test about his favorite football club. Saskia scored 43.5 out of 50, which resulted in him not dumping her. Saskia scored 87%, but her boyfriend provided feedback suggesting she could improve on specific questions and learn player positions. She answered questions about the 2014 FA Cup final, including the scoreline and the winning goalscorer. She also struggled with naming the starting 11 squad and player positions. In her own words, she compared Alexis Sanchez to Eden Hazard, stating Sanchez was "buff" and scored many goals, while Hazard was a "p***k." She also answered his question about why Arsenal is the best team by saying they have won many FA Cups and Thierry Henry is a legend.

Manchester United manager Louis van Gaal is dreaming of beating rivals Manchester City in the Sunday derby at Old Trafford, but he has ruled out both Robin van Persie and Luke Shaw due to not being fit enough to play. Van Gaal stated that winning against City is a big step up the table, potentially securing third place and almost certainly qualifying for the top four, which is better than the pre-season goal. He acknowledged City will be a stern challenge and emphasized the need for his team to control their aggression, noting that he is looking forward to the derby atmosphere at Old Trafford for the first time since arriving.

Arsenal and Liverpool fans protested against rising ticket prices by leaving their seats empty for the first 10 minutes of their lunchtime Premier League clash at the Emirates Stadium. The protest followed the announcement of the Premier League's £5.14 billion TV rights deal, with tickets starting at £64 for the 12:45 pm kick-off. Fans from both clubs, including groups like Arsenal's black scarf movement and Liverpool's Spirit of Shankly and Spion Kop 1906, held banners inside and outside the stadium to raise awareness of the financial struggles fans face.

Chelsea players, including Eden Hazard and Nathan Ake, participated in Audi's football challenge. In the first round, Hazard and Ake won 5-3 by firing balls into a car boot. In the second round, Hazard and Ake won 6-0 after playing over a £127,000 Audi R8 V10 Plus used as a makeshift tennis net. In the final round, Loic Remy and Willian won by shooting at cars from long range, though Willian smashed the wing mirror off one of the Audi cars during the challenge.

Lacey Spears, convicted of second-degree murder for poisoning her five-year-old son, Garnett-Paul Spears, with salt, was sentenced to 20 years to life in prison. Her ex-husband, Chris Hill, expressed anger on Facebook after her sentencing, hoping she would die in prison and criticizing her lack of emotion during the proceedings. The New York judge noted that Spears suffers from a mental illness and described the crime as "unfathomable in its cruelty." Prosecutors blamed Spears for her son's suffering, stating she loaded his feeding tube with salt and used his medical issues to self-aggrandize herself. Spears' lawyer, Stephen Riebling, argued for her innocence and plans to appeal the verdict.

Sabeen Mahmud, a figurehead for humanism, love, and tolerance in Pakistan, was shot dead at point-blank range in Karachi after locking up her second-floor cafe, T2F, for the night. Mahmud was known for hosting discussions on technology, human rights, and women's entrepreneurship, and for introducing people to topics like Jimi Hendrix and street art. Her death occurred after she had just finished a discussion group on a topic many want silenced, specifically regarding the situation in Balochistan, where she had expressed concern about the lack of space for debate in Pakistani media and academia. No one has claimed responsibility for the shooting, and police have not named a motive.

Burlesque performer Lillian Bustle, from New Jersey, is working to eradicate negativity surrounding the word "fat" by embracing it as an honest, body-positive self-descriptor, similar to how she uses "short" and "wife." During a TED talk, she argued that "fat" should not be synonymous with "ugly," noting that while size discrimination in the workplace has risen 66% in 30 years, exposure to body diversity can increase tolerance and acceptance of different body types. Bustle performs burlesque to expose audiences to a "fat" body in a positive, glamorous way, hoping to change perceptions. She began performing in 2012, finding the experience empowering and body-positive, and recommends others find a "courage reference" moment to use during times of insecurity. Despite some negative comments, her TED talk has received mostly positive feedback, including messages from people who reevaluated their views on their bodies after watching.

Anorexic schoolgirl Laura Scurr, aged 15, developed anorexia after feeling too big and being bullied, leading her to become obsessed with being a "size zero." She began restricting her food intake, sometimes surviving on just one piece of fruit a day, and hiding food. This obsession led to her body shutting down, causing her to collapse and be rushed to intensive care. After a week on a heart monitor, she began recovery with eating disorder teams. Today, Laura has improved her body image and confidence, reaching the semi-final of Miss Teen GB, a competition that aims to move away from size zero stereotypes.

A team from the University of Manchester, led by Dr. Sarah Bridle, has produced the largest single high-definition map of mysterious dark matter. This map, which covers 0.4 per cent of the sky, is part of a series intended to eventually provide a 3D view of dark matter across one eighth of the night sky. The map was created using data from the Dark Energy Camera (DECam) on the Victor M. Blanco Telescope at the Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO) in Chile, as part of the five-year Dark Energy Survey (DES).

The survey aims to map 12.5 per cent of the sky over five years. By studying the gravitational effects of dark matter on galaxies, astronomers can map its predicted amounts and study how galaxies formed in the universe. Dark matter, which makes up at least 80 per cent of the matter in the known universe, is invisible but its gravitational pull distorts light, a phenomenon known as gravitational lensing. Analysis of dark matter clumpiness will also help probe the nature of dark energy.

Pablo Mandado (27, Spanish) and Ilze Zebolde (31, Latvian) are cyclists who quit their restaurant jobs in Manchester to embark on an open-ended journey around the world. They started in London, traveled through Europe, and have recently traversed Turkey, Georgia, and Armenia, with plans to continue into Asia and cycle across the American continent.

A leading expert suggests that smartphone use may be responsible for a decline in the frequency of sex among couples. Research indicates that the frequency of sex among Britons has decreased since the internet's emergence, dropping from five times a month in 1990 and four times in 2000 to an average of three times a month for a typical heterosexual couple. Professor David Spiegelhalter attributes this decline to the blurring boundaries between public and private life due to constant technological connectivity, which has made lives busier and squeezed out time spent with partners. Additionally, an increasing number of competing demands on time means sex is falling down priorities, and late-evening work emails can prevent couples from focusing on each other at bedtime.

This is the first sighting of the species in WA and the second in Australia. The 5.68 m juvenile female was identified using DNA profiling. The find is significant because little was known about the species, which was only described in scientific journals in 2003 and is restricted to tropical and subtropical waters. The whale is usually found in Indonesian waters, the Philippines, and the Sea of Japan. Omura's whales have a sleek body shape and several unique skeletal features, including 53 vertebrae and four digits on each pectoral fin. The carcass has been buried, and the skeleton will be recovered in a few years for further investigation.

A team from the University of Manchester, led by Dr. Sarah Bridle, has produced the largest single high-definition map of mysterious dark matter. This map, which covers 0.4 per cent of the sky, is part of a series intended to eventually provide a 3D view of dark matter across one eighth of the night sky. The map was created using data from the dark energy camera, a 57070-megapixel imaging device that is the primary instrument for the dark energy survey (des) led by fermilab in the us.

The survey aims to map 125 per cent of the entire sky over five years. By studying the gravitational effects of dark matter on galaxies, astronomers can map its predicted amounts and study how galaxies formed in the universe. Dark matter, which makes up at least 80 per cent of the matter in the known universe, is invisible but its gravitational pull distorts light, a phenomenon known as gravitational lensing. Analysis of dark matter clumpiness will also help probe the nature of dark energy.
